Can Frontier Agents Solve Diverse, Long-Horizon AI Infrastructure Tasks?

Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization

November 10, 2026
Homepage GitHub Docker Hub

TL;DR. Infrathon evaluates frontier agents on real-world AI infrastructure tasks over 12–24 hours. Claude Opus 5.5 leads six models with a mean rank score of 91.2. Agents can also discover better solutions: Claude raises mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86×, with better video quality. At equal GPU-hours, longer runs are more effective for module and system tasks, while multiple short runs remain competitive on operators.

AI infrastructure determines how efficiently models are trained and served. Optimizing it involves work on individual operations (operators), interacting components (modules), and complete training or serving workflows (systems). Engineers identify bottlenecks, revise code, and measure the result. Each change must preserve correctness, and improving one component can shift the bottleneck elsewhere.

Agents could automate this cycle by using test feedback to choose the next code change. They need to recover from failed experiments and keep searching when early attempts produce little improvement. A short run may end before these revisions produce a better solution.

What Do Existing Benchmarks Measure?

Existing benchmarks differ in task coverage, run duration, and available GPU tasks. KernelBench [1] evaluates operators and modules, while InferenceBench [2] focuses on complete inference services. Φ-Bench [3] covers all three levels, but most tasks use 1.5-hour budgets. EdgeBench [4] supports long runs across broader domains; its open-source release does not include GPU tasks.

Together, these gaps leave an open question: can frontier agents keep improving real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons?

To study this, we construct Infrathon’s 25 tasks with human experts using Infrathon-build, drawing on open-source infrastructure and research projects. 11 operator-level tasks optimize computational primitives with 12-hour budgets; 5 module-level tasks optimize interacting components with 24-hour budgets; and 9 system-level tasks optimize end-to-end training or serving workflows with 24-hour budgets. Infrathon is the first benchmark for long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization across three levels, with 12–24-hour budgets and metrics like TFLOP/s without fixed upper bounds.

Each task specifies a workspace, public tests, private tests, resources, and time budget. Agents develop solutions and run public tests in the Work environment. The Controller checks instruction following and reward hacking before accepted solutions reach the Judge environment for private tests. Feedback guides further revisions throughout the run.

KVzip KV Scoring is one example:

1️⃣ Claude Opus 5.5 leads all six models with a mean rank score of 91.2.

We evaluate six models on all 25 tasks, yielding 150 runs and over 10,000 GPU-hours. Each run reports its highest valid private test score within the time budget. Because tasks use different metrics, we aggregate within-task ranks with equal task weights.

Final model rankings across all 25 tasks

Mean rank scores range from 0 to 100; 100 means first place on every task.

Claude wins nine of the 11 operator tasks, two of the five module tasks, and six of the nine system tasks.

2️⃣ Infrathon can support knowledge discovery

On Quant-VideoGen KV Codec [14], agents compress the attention keys and values cached during video generation. We compare the codec developed by Claude Opus 5.5 during its 24-hour run with the human codec from Quant-VideoGen. Evaluation uses HY-WorldPlay [15] on WorldScore [16] and LongCat-Video [17] on MovieGen [18], with 200 samples per dataset and fixed generation settings across codecs.

Claude increases mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86×, while improving video quality: higher mean PSNR and SSIM, and lower mean LPIPS on both datasets.

Human versus Claude codec compression and video quality
Dataset / video modelCompression (×) ↑PSNR (dB) ↑SSIM ↑LPIPS ↓
WorldScoreHY-WorldPlay6.75 → 20.8931.15 → 36.330.923 → 0.9750.059 → 0.023
MovieGenLongCat-Video6.88 → 18.8323.67 → 26.950.836 → 0.8840.126 → 0.085

Mean values: Human → Claude. Quality metrics use the uncompressed BF16 reference.

The human codec quantizes the residuals left after clustering the cache one value at a time. Claude instead transforms the residuals using principal component analysis and applies entropy coding after quantization.

The two LongCat-Video examples show clearer facial details and mushroom textures with Claude’s codec than with the human codec.

3️⃣ Long Horizon vs. Short Horizon

We evaluate GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on six tasks with equal GPU-hour budgets, using one training and one inference task at each optimization level. Long-horizon optimization uses one T-hour run; short-horizon best-of-n test-time scaling (TTS) uses n independent T/n-hour runs, with n = 2 or 4. Here T is 12 hours for operators and 24 hours for modules and systems.

Longer horizons are more effective for module and system tasks, while short-horizon TTS remains competitive on operators.

Best of two or four short runs relative to one long run at equal GPU-hours
Task levelBest of two / one long runBest of four / one long run
Operator101.3%102.6%
Module96.5%96.9%
System79.4%77.3%

Geometric means of task–model score ratios. 100% means equal performance at equal total GPU-hours.

The long-horizon setting wins nine of 12 comparisons, including all four system comparisons.
